restatements.text: Makes assault on an on-duty hospital worker a felony and increases the maximum penalty to three years in prison, compared to the current one-year maximum in jail.

findings.direction: increases maximum sentences for assaults on hospital workers
findings.quote: Assault on an on-duty hospital worker is a felony punishable by up to three years in prison.
findings.mechanism: Reclassifies the crime as a felony and extends the maximum possible incarceration period from one year to three years for this specific offense.

analysis.answer: Under current law, assault is punishable by up to one year in jail. This measure creates a specific felony for assaulting an on-duty hospital worker, raising the maximum penalty to three years in prison.

It incurs direct costs for the state by potentially increasing the number of people sent to prison and extending their stays. It may also raise the costs of trials and public defense, as felony cases typically require more resources than misdemeanors.
Taxpayers bear the increased costs of the criminal justice system and state prisons. Hospital workers are the intended beneficiaries of any resulting deterrence or incapacitation of offenders.
Prosecutors may use the threat of a three-year felony sentence as leverage during plea negotiations to secure convictions.
The text addresses the problem of assaults on hospital workers. It relies on the mechanism of harsher criminal penalties to incapacitate offenders and deter future assaults.
Prosecutors gain leverage and discretion in charging decisions and plea bargaining by having a felony charge available for this specific type of assault.

The deterrence effect of increasing maximum sentence lengths is disputed among researchers; some find that longer sentences deter crime, while others conclude that the certainty of apprehension is a stronger deterrent than the severity of the punishment.
